title: Weak Mixing and the Chacon Transformation

items.title: Unitary eigenfunction for a probability system
items.statement: For a measure-preserving probability system, an eigenfunction is a nonzero complex L2 class f with U_T f=lambda f. A nonconstant eigenfunction means a class not in C1. The pairing is <f,g>=integral f conjugate(g), linear in the first variable. U_T is unitary when the system is invertible modulo null sets; in general it is an isometry. H0={f: integral f=0}. Completed Lebesgue probability spaces here have the usual modulo-null interval-and-atoms convention; no classification theorem is invoked.
items.strategy: Fix representative-independent class language. Norm preservation gives |lambda|=1. Integrability of f follows from Cauchy–Schwarz with 1. The integral functional is continuous, so H0 is a closed subspace. Subtract the mean only when lambda=1; if lambda differs from 1, integral invariance forces the mean to vanish. No choice beyond the given measure-space objects is needed.

items.title: L two operator conventions for weak mixing
items.statement: For a closed complex L2 subspace H, bounded means linear with ||Af||<=C||f||; ||A||=sup_{||f||<=1}||Af||. Compact means bounded and every bounded sequence has an image subsequence convergent in norm in H. An adjoint A* satisfies <Af,g>=<f,A*g>; self-adjoint means <Af,g>=<f,Ag>, positive means <Af,f>>=0 for all f. An isometry preserves the norm and inner product; a unitary is a surjective isometry. A subspace E is invariant if U(E) is contained in E. Orthogonality and orthogonal complements refer to the fixed first-variable-linear pairing.
items.strategy: These are local L2 conventions, not an appeal to later operator theory. Uniqueness of an adjoint follows by testing the difference against itself. No assertion of adjoint existence is made here. Inner-product preservation for linear isometries follows by expansion of norms of f+g and f+i g. Definitions of positive and self-adjoint are used together when a positive self-adjoint operator is required.

items.title: Closed l two subspaces have orthogonal projections
items.statement: Assume AC. Every closed linear subspace M of complex L2(mu) admits a unique linear contraction P_M with f-P_M f orthogonal to M, P_M f in M, and ||f-P_M f||=inf_{g in M}||f-g||. Thus L2=M direct-sum M-perp. This holds also inside a closed L2 subspace.
items.strategy: AC selects g_n in M with ||f-g_n||²<d²+1/n. Derive the complex parallelogram identity by sesquilinear expansion from the declared complex pairing (the published real parallelogram proof is not a complex proof). The identity gives ||g_n-g_m||²<=2||f-g_n||²+2||f-g_m||²-4d², so completeness and closedness give g in M attaining d. Vary g by t h and i t h for real t to obtain <f-g,h>=0 for every h in M. Orthogonality implies uniqueness, linearity, and ||P_M f||<=||f|| by the Pythagorean expansion. Orthogonal complements are closed because each pairing is continuous. Apply the same argument to a closed subspace H, whose Cauchy sequences converge within H. AC is used only for minimizing sequences and inherited L2 completeness.

items.title: Hilbert cesaro averages converge to the fixed subspace
items.statement: Assume AC. For any linear isometry U on a closed complex L2 subspace H, A_N f=N^{-1}sum_{n=0}^{N-1} U^n f converges in norm to P_F f, F=ker(I-U). In particular this holds for a unitary Koopman operator. The range of U is closed; the map V=U^{-1}P_range(U) is a contraction with <Uf,g>=<f,Vg> and VU=I.
items.strategy: Closedness of range follows by pulling a Cauchy sequence U f_n back to f_n and using completeness inherited through projection. Range projection defines V without an abstract Riesz theorem. For z=P_range(U)g=Uh, <Uf,g>=<Uf,Uh>=<f,h>, hence V is the adjoint, and VU=I. Put M=closure((I-U)H). If h perpendicular to M, <h,h-Uh>=0 and ||Uh||=||h|| imply ||h-Uh||²=0; conversely Uh=h implies <h,g-Ug>=0 by isometry. Thus M-perp=F and projection gives H=M direct-sum F. A_N(I-U)g=(g-U^N g)/N tends to zero; ||A_N||<=1 extends this to M. On F all averages are identity. The limit is the orthogonal projection, not an unspecified invariant vector. AC is inherited from projection/completeness.

items.title: Product rectangle kernels are dense in complex l two
items.statement: Assume AC. On the completed product of two finite measure spaces, finite complex linear combinations of rectangle indicators 1_E(x)1_F(y) are dense in complex L2. In particular, if a kernel pairs to zero against every rectangle indicator it is zero in L2.
items.strategy: Apply the real-valued completion representative theorem separately to the real and imaginary components, replace their exceptional infinite values by zero, and combine to obtain a product-measurable complex representative using the completion theorem (AC supplies its countable choices). Approximate in L2 by a finite complex simple function. Approximate each of its finitely many measurable sets in symmetric difference by the rectangle algebra; ||1_E-1_R||² equals the symmetric-difference measure. Choose each tolerance so the coefficient-weighted sum of square-root errors is below the target. Disjointify finite rectangle unions. The zero-pairing assertion follows by taking an approximant R to k and |<k,k>|=|<k,k-R>|<=||k||||k-R||. This avoids an invalid exchange of the quantifiers for almost-everywhere sections.

references.title: Axler 10.70 p.314; local generating-algebra proof replaces the last section-quantifier step

items.title: Square integrable kernels define bounded compact integral operators
items.statement: Assume AC. For a probability space and k in complex L2 of its completed square, Kf(x)=integral k(x,y)f(y)dmu(y) defines a representative-independent bounded compact linear operator on L2, with ||K||<=||k||2. A zero operator K forces k=0. Finite-rank approximation is in operator norm.
items.strategy: First use completed Tonelli on |k|²: sections are square integrable almost everywhere. Cauchy–Schwarz gives |Kf(x)|²<=(integral |k(x,y)|²dy)||f||² and therefore ||Kf||<=||k||||f||. On a probability square |k(x,y)f(y)| is integrable by product Cauchy–Schwarz, so Fubini gives measurability; use the zero extension on exceptional parameters. Null changes do not alter the resulting class by Tonelli. Rectangle kernels have finite-dimensional range. Build a finite orthonormal basis by the finite Gram–Schmidt subtraction/normalization algorithm; coordinates of images of a bounded sequence are bounded, so apply real Bolzano–Weierstrass successively to the real and imaginary parts of the finitely many coordinates, retaining subsequences at each step. All coordinates then converge and their finite basis sum converges in L2. Approximate k by rectangle kernels k_m; ||K-K_m||<=||k-k_m||. Successively choose nested subsequences for K_m (AC) and take a diagonal subsequence; for fixed m the image error under K is bounded by two operator-norm errors plus the K_m Cauchy error. Completeness gives convergence. If K=0 then <K1_F,1_E>=integral_{E x F}k=0 for all rectangles; apply rectangle density. This also proves the norm-limit compactness fact needed later, without citing the later compact-operator page.

items.title: Conjugate transpose kernels give adjoints
items.statement: Assume AC. If K is the kernel operator of k, its adjoint is the kernel operator of k*(x,y)=conjugate(k(y,x)); ||K*||=||K||, and (K*)*=K. Both are compact.
items.strategy: Swap the factors on rectangles, extend integral invariance to the product sigma-algebra and its completion by the rectangle approximation and null-set description; thus ||k*||2=||k||2. For f,g the absolute double integral of k(x,y)f(y)conjugate(g(x)) is bounded by ||k||2||f||2||g||2, since the product function has squared norm ||f||²||g||². Fubini gives <Kf,g>=<f,K*g>, with conjugation in the correct place. Uniqueness tests against each difference vector. From ||z||=sup_{||g||<=1}|<z,g>| (test g=z/||z||) obtain ||K||<=||K*|| and the reverse by double adjoint. Compactness is the kernel lemma, not the general assertion that adjoints preserve compactness.

items.title: Invariant square integrable kernel produces a compact intertwiner
items.statement: Assume AC. If T preserves a completed Lebesgue probability space and k(Tx,Ty)=k(x,y) a.e., its kernel operator K is compact and KU=UK, K*U=UK*, for U=U_T, even when U is only an isometry. If k has zero integrals in each variable a.e., K1=K*1=0 and K,K* preserve H0. Nonzero k gives nonzero restriction to H0 in this case.
items.strategy: Prove T x T preserves the uncompleted product from rectangles and the generating-pi-system theorem. Its preimages of completed null subsets lie in product-measurable null preimages, so it also acts on the completion. Its Koopman pullback W is an isometry. Let V=U* supplied explicitly by the range-projection formula in the mean lemma. For a rectangle tensor k=a(x)b(y), check K_{Wk}=U K_k V: integral b(Ty)f(y)=<f,U conjugate(b)>=<Vf,conjugate(b)>. Extend to all kernels by rectangle density and the kernel norm estimate. Invariance gives K=UKV, hence KU=UK since VU=I. The conjugate-transpose kernel is also W-invariant, so the same calculation gives K*U=UK*. Zero marginals give K1=K*1=0; then <Kf,1>=<f,K*1>=0, and similarly for K*. Since every f is its mean plus an H0 vector, nonzero K with K1=0 has nonzero H0 restriction. No inverse of a noninvertible transformation is assumed.

references.title: Sarig Theorem 3.2 p.91 (criterion); Axler Example 10.5 p.282 (kernel formula)
Axler Example 10.5 and 10.70; intertwining derived locally

items.title: Nonzero compact kernel operators yield nonzero positive compact k star k
items.statement: Assume AC. For a nonzero compact kernel operator K with K1=K*1=0, S=K*K on H0 is bounded, compact, self-adjoint, positive and nonzero. If K and K* commute with a Koopman isometry U then SU=US.
items.strategy: Adjoint identity gives <Sf,g>=<Kf,Kg>=<f,Sg>, and <Sf,f>=||Kf||². Choose f in H0 with Kf nonzero, so S is nonzero. Boundedness follows from composition; a bounded sequence has a subsequence whose K images converge, and the continuous K* preserves that convergence, proving compactness of S. Multiply the two commutation identities. No claim is made that K itself has a nonzero eigenvalue.

references.title: Axler Example 10.5; 10.69(b) p.313 and 10.96 p.326; direct K-star-K argument

items.title: Nonzero positive compact self adjoint operators have positive finite dimensional eigenspaces
items.statement: Assume AC. On a nonzero closed complex L2 subspace H, every nonzero bounded positive self-adjoint compact operator S has a positive eigenvalue alpha=||S||; its alpha-eigenspace is nonzero, closed and finite-dimensional.
items.strategy: Set alpha=sup_{||x||=1}<Sx,x>. Positivity of <S(x+t y),x+t y> for complex t proves |<Sx,y>|²<=<Sx,x><Sy,y> by minimizing the scalar quadratic (zero diagonal case follows by arbitrary small real/imaginary t). Taking sup over unit y gives ||Sx||²<=alpha<Sx,x>; hence ||S||<=alpha, while the reverse is immediate. If alpha=0 then S=0 by this estimate, so alpha>0. Use AC to select unit x_n with <Sx_n,x_n> tending to alpha. Expand ||Sx_n-alpha x_n||²<=alpha(alpha-<Sx_n,x_n>) tending to zero. Compactness gives Sx_nj tending to y; thus x_nj tends to x=y/alpha with ||x||=1, and continuity gives Sx=alpha x. The eigenspace is closed as a kernel. If it had no finite spanning set, AC and finite Gram–Schmidt recursively give an infinite orthonormal sequence in it; its S-images are pairwise distance alpha sqrt(2), contradicting compactness. This proves the needed eigenvalue fact without the Fredholm alternative, weak compactness, general spectral theorem or Zorn basis.

references.title: Axler 10.96–10.99 p.326, with local positive quadratic argument replacing Fredholm theory

items.title: Compact intertwiners produce finite dimensional invariant subspaces
items.statement: Assume AC. A nonzero invariant square-integrable kernel with zero marginals produces a nonzero finite-dimensional U-invariant subspace E of H0, and U restricted to E is unitary.
items.strategy: Take the positive alpha-eigenspace of K*K in H0. Commutation gives S(Uf)=U(Sf)=alpha Uf, so U(E) is contained in E. U is injective because it is an isometry. On a finite-dimensional vector space an injective endomorphism is surjective (apply a basis and linear independence, or rank-nullity); therefore U|E is unitary. This works also for noninvertible T and never requires unitary invariance of all H0.

references.title: Sarig Theorem 3.2 p.91, local compact-intertwiner proof of its difficult implication

items.title: Nonzero finite dimensional complex invariant subspaces have unitary eigenvectors
items.statement: Every nonzero finite-dimensional complex subspace E invariant under a Koopman isometry contains a nonzero eigenvector f of U, with |lambda|=1. If E is contained in H0, f is nonconstant.
items.strategy: The minimum-modulus theorem proves every nonconstant polynomial in C[z] has a root, so C satisfies exactly the algebraically-closed-field hypothesis of the declared finite-dimensional eigenvalue corollary. Apply the corollary to U|E. Alternatively its proof takes a root of the monic degree-d characteristic polynomial and uses singularity of U-lambda I to obtain a nonzero kernel vector; keep those transitive suppliers explicit in examined evidence. Norm preservation gives |lambda|=1. A constant mean-zero class is zero, hence this nonzero f cannot be constant. Only finitely many choices of a basis and eigenvector are made here; AC is inherited if E is obtained from the preceding compact lemma.

references.title: Sarig Definition 3.3 p.90; finite-dimensional eigenvalue interface proved by the published characteristic-polynomial and minimum-modulus suppliers

items.title: Weak mixing is equivalent to absence of nonconstant eigenfunctions
items.statement: Assume AC. For a measure-preserving transformation T on a completed Lebesgue probability space, the following are equivalent: absolute-Cesaro weak mixing; absence of nonconstant complex L2 eigenfunctions; ergodicity of T x T on the completed product. No invertibility hypothesis is needed. The library definition remains the absolute-Cesaro definition.
items.strategy: Weak mixing excludes an eigenfunction: after centering a lambda=1 eigenfunction (lambda!=1 already has mean zero), |<U^n f,f>|=||f||² for all n, contradicting the published L2 correlation criterion. Conversely absence of nonconstant eigenfunctions first implies ergodicity by invariant indicators. If W=U_(T x T) has a nonconstant invariant kernel k, subtract its total mean. Its kernel K is nonzero by rectangle density. K1 and K*1 are invariant by intertwining, hence constant by ergodicity; their integrals are zero, so both vanish. Thus K is nonzero on H0 and the K*K finite-dimensional invariant-subspace lemma plus the complex eigenvector lemma produce a nonconstant eigenfunction, contradiction. All W-fixed classes are therefore constants. Apply the local mean lemma on the completed product to F(x,y)=f0(x)conjugate(f0(y)), where f0=f-integral f. For G(x,y)=g(x)conjugate(g(y)), Fubini gives <W^n F,G>=|<U^n f0,g>|². Integral F=|integral f0|²=0, so its Cesaro pairing tends to zero. Finite Cauchy–Schwarz then gives average |<U^n f0,g>| <= sqrt(average |<U^n f0,g>|²), establishing absolute-Cesaro correlations and hence the set definition. Product ergodicity implies no eigenfunctions because f0(x)conjugate(f0(y)) is a nonzero invariant kernel of total mean zero. Conversely no eigenfunctions already showed product ergodicity. For completeness, the harvested density-zero variant follows by thresholds {n:a_n>1/j}: choose cutoffs N_j with density of that threshold below 1/j for N>=N_j, and take the union of each threshold in [N_j,N_(j+1)); nested thresholds bound the resulting exceptional density. The converse follows by bounding the exceptional part of a bounded sequence. No spectral measures, recurrence, or recorded results enter.

references.title: Sarig Theorem 3.2 pp.91–92; local Hilbert and compact-kernel route supplies implication omitted there

items.title: Chacon three cut one spacer towers
items.statement: Assume AC for the Lebesgue measure assertions. Start with the ordered one-level tower L_(0,0)=[0,2/3) and reservoir R0=[2/3,1). At stage r divide every level into its left, middle and right thirds; stack first the left column, then the middle column, then a spacer of width w_(r+1) cut from the left end of R_r, then the right column. The tower order defines translations between consecutive levels, leaving its top undefined. h0=1, h_(r+1)=3h_r+1, w_r=2/3^(r+1), h_r=(3^(r+1)-1)/2. Tower mass is 1-3^(-r-1), reservoir mass 3^(-r-1). No limit map is claimed in this definition.
items.strategy: Give a literal finite ordered list of half-open physical subintervals at each stage. Within a column preserve the old order. New spacer is [1-3^(-r-1),1-3^(-r-2)); its length is w_(r+1), and it lies in the reservoir. Induct on r to check distinct levels, width and the two displayed closed forms. The union of levels and the reservoir is [0,1). Finite recursion, widths and geometric arithmetic are choice-free. The assertions about actual Lebesgue measures use the box theorem, whose Countable Choice hypothesis is supplied by AC here, even at finite stages.

items.title: Chacon partial maps extend to an invertible map mod null sets
items.statement: Assume AC. The compatible partial translations of the normalized Chacon towers determine an invertible Lebesgue-probability-preserving transformation modulo null sets: there is an invariant measurable conull X0 on which the map and its inverse are defined and measurable. The ambient map may be extended by identity off X0; no everywhere interval-bijection formula for the tower limit is asserted.
items.strategy: Let D_r be tower minus its top and E_r tower minus its base. Each partial map is a finite disjoint union of equal-width translations, hence a measurable measure-preserving bijection D_r to E_r. At the next stage existing arrows merely restrict to thirds; new arrows join old column tops, spacer and next bases, so domains/ranges increase and maps agree. Their complements have mass reservoir+w_r=3^(-r), tending to zero. The union map T:D to E, D=union D_r,E=union E_r, is a bijection, as compatibility also holds for inverse maps. It and its inverse are countably piecewise translations; measure preservation follows by partitioning into first-domain pieces. Remove the exceptional set [0,1) minus (D intersection E) and all its forward/backward images under all finite defined iterates; each is measurable null, so their countable union is null. Its complement X0 is invariant and both directions are everywhere defined there. Extend identity on the null complement only if an ambient total measurable map is desired. AC supplies the inherited Lebesgue countable-additivity assumptions, not arbitrary pointwise inverses.

items.title: Chacon levels approximate measurable sets
items.statement: Assume AC. Every Lebesgue-measurable subset of [0,1) is approximable in symmetric-difference measure by a union of levels of a sufficiently late Chacon tower; the error tends to zero with stage. Functions constant on levels and zero off the tower are dense in complex L2. For any positive-measure E and delta>0, some sufficiently late level J satisfies mu(E intersection J)>(1-delta)mu(J).
items.strategy: The partition consisting of tower levels plus the reservoir refines at every stage and has maximal physical interval length max(w_r,3^(-r-1)) tending to zero. Finite unions of physical intervals form an algebra generating the trace Borel sigma-algebra. Approximate a Borel representative of E by a finite interval union using the published finite-measure generating-algebra lemma. Each endpoint intersects at most two atoms; replacing that union by contained atoms loses at most the number of endpoints times the mesh. Discard the reservoir, of vanishing measure. Completion changes no error. Refinement shows the same estimate for every later stage. For simple functions approximate their finitely many indicator sets and then apply finite-simple L2 density. For the last assertion choose a level union Q with error eta much smaller than delta mu(E). If each selected level had E-proportion <=1-delta, then mu(Q minus E)>=delta mu(Q), contradicting eta and mu(Q)>=mu(E)-eta. This proves the high-density-level fact without Lebesgue differentiation or Lusin. AC is inherited from the completion representative and Lebesgue measure suppliers.

items.title: Chacon transformation is ergodic
items.statement: Assume AC. The normalized Chacon transformation is ergodic.
items.strategy: For an invariant-mod-null E of positive measure, take a level J in tower r with E-density >1-delta, with r arbitrarily large. The maps T^j between each pair of levels preserve measure and E modulo null sets, so all levels of that tower have the same E-density. Thus mu(E)>=(1-delta)mu(tower_r). Let r tend to infinity and delta to zero, yielding mu(E)=1. For strict invariant sets the hypothesis holds in particular; hence the library definition of ergodicity is met. All comparisons occur on the invariant conull X0, so deleted null sets do not affect them.

references.title: Katok–Thouvenot rank-one generating partitions paragraph p.697, expanded local ergodicity argument

items.title: Chacon eigenfunctions are constant
items.statement: Assume AC. Every complex L2 eigenfunction of the normalized Chacon transformation is constant almost everywhere; its eigenvalue is 1.
items.strategy: By isometry |lambda|=1. Then |f| is invariant; ergodicity makes it a positive constant, so rescale to |f|=1. For epsilon>0 partition the unit circle into finitely many measurable sets of diameter <epsilon. Some inverse image E has positive measure; choose a unit a with |f-a|<epsilon on E. The high-density-level lemma gives J with mu(J minus E)<delta mu(J), delta<1/6. In tower r+1, T^h_r maps the left third J_L onto J_M, and T^(h_r+1) maps J_M onto J_R. For the first map, at most 2delta mu(J) of J_L is excluded by requiring both x and its image to be in E; since mu(J_L)=mu(J)/3, a positive-measure good set remains. On it |lambda^h_r a-a|<=2epsilon. Similarly |lambda^(h_r+1)a-a|<=2epsilon from J_M to J_R. Thus |lambda-1|<=4epsilon; let epsilon tend to zero. Now f is invariant and the invariant-function theorem makes it constant a.e. This argument works with an arbitrary level, avoids dividing by a possibly zero approximate value, and supplies the step left as Exercise 6.3 by Creutz. All eigenfunction equations are restricted off the countable union of their iterate-exception sets.

references.title: Creutz Theorem 6.11 and Exercise 6.3 pp.42–43 (incomplete source; local completion above)

items.title: Chacon tower height correlations obstruct mixing
items.statement: Assume AC. Let A=L_(1,0)=[0,2/9), of measure 2/9. For every r>=1, mu(A intersection T^(-h_r) A)>=2/27>4/81=mu(A)^2. Hence the tower-height subsequence obstructs strong mixing. More generally liminf_r mu(E intersection T^(-h_r)E)>=mu(E)/3 for every measurable E.
items.strategy: For any union Q of tower-r levels, the union of their left thirds has measure mu(Q)/3 and T^h_r maps it into the corresponding middle thirds, all still inside Q. This proves the lower bound for Q at stage r. The fixed initial next-stage base A is a union of descendant levels of every tower r>=1; thus the exact bound holds for all those r, without treating a moving set as a mixing witness. Since h_r increases to infinity and 2/27=6/81>4/81, correlations fail to approach the product. For general E approximate it by Q_r with symmetric difference eta_r tending to zero. Measure preservation bounds correlation error by 2eta_r, and |mu(Q_r)-mu(E)|<=eta_r, giving lower bound mu(E)/3-(7/3)eta_r. Take liminf. No false claim of an exact limiting correlation is made.

items.title: Chacon transformation is weakly mixing but not mixing
items.statement: Assume AC. There exists an invertible completed Lebesgue probability system, the normalized three-cut one-spacer Chacon transformation, which is weakly mixing in the absolute-Cesaro sense but is not strongly mixing.
items.strategy: The extension lemma supplies the required actual conull invertible probability system. Every complex L2 eigenfunction is constant by the local eigenfunction proof; apply the locally proved absolute-Cesaro spectral equivalence. The fixed set A=[0,2/9) and h_r subsequence from the correlation lemma contradict strong mixing. Keep all four interfaces visible and carry the AC assumptions of their constructions.

items.title: Weak mixing implies strong mixing
items.statement: False claim: every weakly mixing probability-preserving transformation is strongly mixing. Under AC the normalized Chacon system refutes it.
items.strategy: Use the final Chacon theorem as the counterexample supplier: it certifies the absolute-Cesaro premise and disproves the strong-mixing conclusion in the same system. Name its witness A=[0,2/9) and h_r, but do not repeat or hide its construction. This false statement remains an A-page conceptual boundary as prescribed by the design.

title: Weak Mixing and the Chacon Transformation — Examples

items.title: First three chacon tower heights
items.statement: The first three normalized Chacon heights are h0=1, h1=4, h2=13; generally h_r=(3^(r+1)-1)/2.
items.strategy: Compute 3 times 1 plus 1 = 4, then 3 times 4 plus 1 = 13. Substitute the closed form into the recurrence and initial value. These are formal finite tower data and do not presuppose readiness of the limit transformation.

items.title: Chacon spacer measure budget
items.statement: Assume AC for interpretation as Lebesgue measures. The initial column has width 2/3. The first two spacers have widths 2/9 and 2/27. The sum of all spacer widths is 1/3, while the unused reservoir after stage r has mass 3^(-r-1), tending to zero. Spacers are retained in subsequent towers; only the unused tail tends to zero.
items.strategy: Sum the finite geometric series sum_{j=1}^r 2/3^(j+1)=1/3-3^(-r-1). Add the initial mass 2/3 to get 1-3^(-r-1). Taking the geometric tail limit establishes the budget; it does not claim total spacer mass tends to zero. This arithmetic is choice-free.

items.title: Chacon correlation subsequence prevents mixing
items.statement: Under AC, A=[0,2/9) in the Chacon system has mu(A)=2/9 and correlations at h_r (r>=1) at least 2/27, exceeding mu(A)^2=4/81. It refutes strong mixing for that system.
items.strategy: Read the fixed set and all-r>=1 inequality from the A-page obstruction lemma. Convert 2/27 to 6/81, subtract 4/81 to obtain a uniform gap 2/81, and use h_r tending to infinity. A subsequence with this gap suffices; existence or value of a subsequential limit is unnecessary.

references.title: Katok–Thouvenot Theorem 5.12 p.697; normalized fixed-level computation
